Abstract written by a model

In A Study in Scarlet, Sherlock Holmes is an eccentric consulting detective who uses scientific knowledge, observation, and deduction to solve the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson and identify Jefferson Hope. In The Sign of the Four, Sherlock Holmes is an unofficial consulting detective who investigates Mary Morstan’s case, solves the Pondicherry Lodge murder, pursues Jonathan Small, and recovers the treasure chest. In The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes is a consulting and professional detective who investigates cases from Baker Street using observation, deduction, disguises, and physical evidence. In The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes is a London consulting detective and unofficial investigator whose cases are chronicled by Dr. Watson, culminating in his confrontation with Professor Moriarty at Reichenbach Falls. In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Sherlock Holmes is a London consulting detective who investigates Sir Charles Baskerville’s death, protects Sir Henry, exposes Jack Stapleton’s plot, and kills the hound. In The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes is a living consulting detective who returns from hiding after surviving the Reichenbach Fall and resumes solving difficult investigations with Dr. Watson. In The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes investigates several cases through physical clues, records, interviews, and traps, including the murder of Peter Carey, while working under the alias Captain Basil. In His Last Bow, Sherlock Holmes is a consulting detective and patriotic agent who solves criminal and national-security cases, later infiltrating a German espionage network under the alias Altamont.

and 2 more works

In The Valley of Fear, Sherlock Holmes is an independent detective who deciphers Porlock’s warning, investigates the apparent murder of John Douglas at Birlstone, and exposes the staged crime and Moriarty’s involvement. In The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes is a fictional consulting and private detective who investigates varied cases, protects victims, and eventually retires to Sussex while continuing to accept investigations.

One sentence for each work Sherlock Holmes is in, in date order. A model wrote them when it joined the works; each title opens that work’s own account below.

In each work

Sherlock Holmes in each of the 10 accounts the graph joined, in date order. Nothing is merged: an abstract, a narrative and a claim stay with the work they were written from.

Sherlock Holmes in A Study in Scarlet

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1886 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a man of eccentric scientific studies, especially chemistry, anatomy, poisons, and postmortem subjects, whose passion is definite and exact knowledge. He works intermittently at a chemical laboratory, discovers a hæmoglobin-based blood-stain test, smokes strong tobacco, plays the violin remarkably and eccentrically, and can be silent or in the dumps. He shares rooms at 221B, Baker Street with Dr. John Watson. Holmes’s trade is consulting detective work. He serves official detectives, private inquiry agencies, and people in trouble through observation, deduction, special knowledge, and analytical reasoning. He is highly trained in such matters as footstep tracing and cigar ashes, and he demonstrates his method early by inferring Watson’s connection with Afghanistan and identifying a visitor’s former occupation. He regards Gregson and Lestrade as inferior in detective work and expects them to seek credit for a solved case. The central action follows Holmes’s investigation of the deaths of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson. At Lauriston Gardens, he studies tracks, footprints, the body, blood, writing, fingernail marks, and cigar ash. He concludes that Drebber was poisoned and reconstructs the murderer as a tall, florid, red-faced man with particular boots, a long right-hand fingernail, and a Trichinopoly cigar, who arrived in a four-wheeled cab. A lost wedding ring becomes bait: Holmes advertises for it, detects a disguised response, interviews John Rance, and pursues the connection. As the investigation expands, Holmes uses street Arabs, telegraphs Cleveland, and tests pills from Stangerson’s room on a terrier, proving that one is poisonous and one harmless. He identifies the cab and its driver, Jefferson Hope, before the arrest, lures Hope into Baker Street, handcuffs him, and helps take him to the police station. Holmes then hears Hope’s account, asks about the person who collected the advertised ring, and explains to Watson how ordinary deductions led to the solution within three days, despite public credit going to Gregson and Lestrade.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

CHAPTER I.

Sherlock Holmes is introduced as an eccentric, highly knowledgeable investigator of chemistry and anatomy who works intermittently in a hospital laboratory. He discovers a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin, demonstrates its use in detecting blood stains, and agrees to share lodgings with Dr. Watson. Holmes correctly infers that Watson has been in Afghanistan without explaining his method.

CHAPTER II.

Sherlock Holmes moves into 221B, Baker Street, with Dr. John Watson and settles into a quiet, highly regular life. He reveals that he is a consulting detective who advises official and private investigators, and he demonstrates his powers of observation and deduction by identifying Watson’s past and a visitor’s former occupation.

CHAPTER III.

Sherlock Holmes receives Tobias Gregson’s report and goes with the Doctor to 3, Lauriston Gardens. He examines the grounds, the body, the room, the blood, and the objects found in Enoch J. Drebber’s pockets, concluding that Drebber was murdered by poison. Holmes deduces that the murderer was a man over six feet tall, in the prime of life, with small feet, coarse square-toed boots, a florid face, long fingernails on his right hand, and a Trichinopoly cigar; he also infers that the man arrived with Drebber in a four-wheeled cab.

CHAPTER IV.

Sherlock Holmes explains that the cab tracks, footprints, stride lengths, writing height, fingernail marks, and cigar ash led him to deductions about the suspects. He interviews John Rance and identifies the tall, red-faced drunken man as the second suspect, believing that the man returned for the ring. Holmes plans to use the ring as bait if necessary and describes the murder as a scarlet thread to be unraveled.

CHAPTER V.

Sherlock Holmes hypothesizes that the murderer lost the wedding ring while bending over Enoch J. Drebber’s body and places an advertisement in Dr. Watson’s name to recover it. He expects the murderer in the brown coat to respond, but instead follows the disguised visitor to Duncan Street and realizes that the apparent old woman was an agile young man.

CHAPTER VI.

Sherlock Holmes reads the newspaper reports with amusement and observes that Gregson and Lestrade will claim credit whether the case succeeds or fails. He employs a group of street Arabs to gather information and listens as Gregson explains his arrest of Arthur Charpentier.

CHAPTER VII.

Sherlock Holmes identifies the connection between the murders of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson through the pills found in Stangerson’s room. He tests the pills on a terrier, discovering that one is deadly poison and the other harmless. Holmes then lures Jefferson Hope into the room, places handcuffs on him, identifies him as the murderer, and helps subdue him.

CHAPTER VI.

Sherlock Holmes helps restrain Jefferson Hope, takes him to the police-station, and invites John Watson, M.D., and the detectives to accompany them. Hope praises Holmes for persistently following his trail.

“That was how Enoch Drebber came to his end. All I had to do then was

Sherlock Holmes listens to Jefferson Hope’s account and asks who collected the ring advertised by Holmes. He praises the unnamed accomplice for acting smartly.

CHAPTER VII.

Sherlock Holmes explains to Doctor Watson how ordinary deductions and analytical reasoning led him from the crime-scene evidence to Jefferson Hope. He identifies Hope as the murderer and former cabdriver, organizes a Street Arab detective corps to find him, and complains that the Echo credits Gregson and Lestrade instead of him.

Sherlock Holmes in The Sign of the Four

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1890-02 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is an unofficial consulting detective and analytical investigator who has made detection his particular profession. He regards himself as the last and highest appeal when official detectives cannot solve a case, relying on observation, deduction, chemical analysis, specialized knowledge such as tobacco ashes, disguises, and irregular methods. He works closely with Dr. John Watson, employs Wiggins and the Baker Street Irregulars, and values cold reason above emotional attachment. When deprived of intellectual work, he abhors stagnation, craves mental exaltation, and uses cocaine as a stimulant. In the Mary Morstan case, Holmes begins by meeting and questioning Miss Morstan about her missing father, pearls, anonymous letters, and a mysterious paper. He connects the handwriting, investigates Major Sholto’s death, recognizes the paper’s significance, and accompanies Morstan and Watson to meet Thaddeus Sholto. At Pondicherry Lodge, he gains entry through his past boxing connection with McMurdo, examines a locked-room murder, identifies poison and the route of escape, and clears Thaddeus Sholto of the killing. Holmes reconstructs the fugitives’ movements from footprints, a rope, a poisoned thorn, and a creosote trail. With Toby’s help, he traces Jonathan Small and an unnamed associate through London, then learns that they escaped in the Aurora. When the search stalls, Holmes advertises, investigates in disguise, recruits the Irregulars, directs Athelney Jones, and locates the launch at Jacobson's Yard. He leads the Thames pursuit, stops the fugitives, recovers the iron chest formerly containing the treasure, and finds evidence of the Islander’s weapon. Afterward, Holmes questions Jonathan Small, offers help if Small tells the truth, and listens to his account with interest but also disgust. He concludes that the full justice of the earlier events cannot be judged without hearing Small’s story. The episode ends with Holmes rejecting marriage as a threat to impartial judgment and reaching again for his cocaine-bottle.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

15 sections; each heading opens the text

The Sign of the Four / Chapter I

Sherlock Holmes takes cocaine and describes himself as the only unofficial consulting detective, working as an expert of last resort for cases that challenge Gregson, Lestrade, and Athelney Jones. He explains his methods through analyses of tobacco ashes, footsteps, hands, Watson’s movements, and Watson’s watch. He agrees to meet Miss Mary Morstan when she arrives at Baker Street.

Chapter II

Sherlock Holmes questions Miss Mary Morstan about her father, the pearls, and the anonymous correspondence. He determines that the handwriting on the letter and the pearl-box addresses belongs to the same person, agrees to attend the Lyceum Theatre meeting, and plans to make further inquiries.

Chapter III

Sherlock Holmes finds that Major Sholto died on April 28, 1882, and reasons that Sholto’s heir may have sent yearly presents to Captain Morstan’s daughter as compensation for knowledge of her father’s fate. He examines the mysterious paper with a double lens, recognizes it as Indian-manufactured paper containing a building plan and unusual writing, and admits that the case is deeper than he first supposed. He carries a revolver and studies London’s streets during the night’s expedition.

Chapter IV

Sherlock Holmes accompanies Miss Morstan and Dr. Watson to meet Thaddeus Sholto and agrees that the information will go no further. He listens closely to Sholto’s account and says that they may be able to throw light on the remaining mystery before urging the party to leave for Norwood.

Chapter V

Sherlock Holmes gains entrance to Pondicherry Lodge by reminding the porter McMurdo of their former boxing match. He examines marks on the stairs and the locked chamber, identifies the death as murder, and recognizes the thorn as poisoned. Holmes tells Thaddeus Sholto to report the matter to the police.

Chapter VI

Sherlock Holmes examines the locked room, window, rope, footprints, creosote, and poisoned thorn, reconstructing how the intruders entered and escaped. He identifies Jonathan Small from the evidence, promises to clear Thaddeus Sholto, and sends Dr. Watson to fetch Toby while he continues investigating.

Chapter VII

Sherlock Holmes examines the footprints, identifies the distinctive separation of the toes, and uses the creasote scent to direct Toby’s pursuit. He deduces that the wooden-legged man is Jonathan Small and that an unnamed associate committed the murder, then follows the trail with Dr. John Watson.

leash and tried to break into a run. I could see by the gleam in

Sherlock Holmes follows Toby to Broderick and Nelson’s large timber-yard. He appears to think they are nearing the end of their journey, then laughs uncontrollably with the narrator when Toby stops at the barrel.

Chapter VIII

Holmes follows Toby’s recovered scent to a wharf and learns from Mrs. Smith that the Aurora was taken away during the night by Mordecai Smith and a wooden-legged man. He recruits Wiggins and the Baker Street Irregulars to search for the launch, studies the clues concerning the second fugitive, and identifies him as probably an Andaman islander.

Chapter IX

Sherlock Holmes is troubled and restless because the search for the fugitives and the steam launch has stalled. He places an advertisement, travels down the river in disguise, and returns disguised as an old sailor after learning enough to arrange a police pursuit. He requires Athelney Jones to follow his orders and plans to capture the men, recover the treasure, and question Jonathan Small.

Chapter X

Sherlock Holmes deduces that Jonathan Small concealed the Aurora at Jacobson's Yard and organizes an ambush there. He leads the pursuit down the Thames, orders the crew to increase speed, and fires at the Islander when he raises a weapon. Afterward, he identifies the recovered iron chest as the one that contained the Sholtos' treasure and finds one of the Islander's darts embedded in the hatchway.

Chapter XI

Sherlock Holmes questions Jonathan Small and offers him a cigar and a drink. Holmes says he believes the poison acted so quickly that Thaddeus Sholto was dead before Small reached the room, and he arranged for Dr. Watson to take the treasure box to Mary Morstan.

Chapter XII

Holmes sits with Jonathan Small after the pursuit and responds calmly to Small’s claims. He observes that they cannot know whether justice was originally on Small’s side until they have heard his story.

He stopped, and held out his manacled hands for the whiskey-and-water

Sherlock Holmes listens with deep interest to Small’s account but shows disgust at Small’s conduct and manner. He sharply tells Small to continue his story.

“A very remarkable account,” said Sherlock Holmes. “A fitting wind-up

Sherlock Holmes questions Jonathan Small about his account and learns that Small brought his own rope and that Tonga had retained one dart in his blow-pipe. He says that emotional attachments oppose the cold reason he values and that he would never marry for fear of biasing his judgment. Holmes identifies Lal Rao as the confederate in the Norwood affair and ends the episode by reaching for his cocaine-bottle.

Sherlock Holmes in The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1891-06-25 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a consulting and professional detective, described by Watson as a reasoning and observing machine and a specialist in crime. From Baker Street, where he has chambers and lodgings and is closely associated with Dr. John Watson, he conducts investigations chiefly for the love of his art rather than wealth. His central methods are disciplined observation, deduction before theorising, examination of physical traces, disguises, and prolonged thought. He is energetic, generally successful, and regarded as a last court of appeal, although his methods may be theoretical and fantastic. He has extraordinary observational and incisive reasoning powers, plays the violin, uses a black clay pipe, keeps newspaper cuttings, and has Bohemian habits; he also habitually uses cocaine, alternating it with ambition. The record unfolds through cases in which Holmes repeatedly converts apparently minor details into solutions. In the Irene Adler matter, he identifies the King of Bohemia, locates the hidden photograph through a staged fire alarm, but finds that Adler has anticipated him; he retains her photograph as his reward. He exposes the Red-Headed League as a diversion for a bank tunnel and captures John Clay. For Mary Sutherland, he proves that James Windibank created the Hosmer Angel deception. In Boscombe Valley, he clears James McCarthy by identifying John Turner and privately preserving Turner’s confession. After John Openshaw’s death, Holmes traces the threatening gang to the Lone Star and seeks to warn its captain. He resolves Neville St. Clair’s supposed disappearance by removing Hugh Boone’s disguise, follows the blue carbuncle through a goose supply chain to James Ryder, and releases Ryder after obtaining his confession. He uncovers Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s snake-based murder scheme at Stoke Moran, identifies a coining gang near Eyford, and explains Hatty Doran’s disappearance by tracing Francis Hay Moulton. He restores the stolen coronet gems and establishes Arthur Holder’s innocence through disguise and physical evidence. Finally, responding to Violet Hunter’s appeal at the Copper Beeches, he deduces that she was meant to impersonate Alice Rucastle, exposes Alice’s imprisonment and escape route, and resolves the remaining mystery through Mrs. Toller’s account. Throughout, Watson is his friend, colleague, assistant, witness, and chronicler.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

37 sections; each heading opens the text

I. A SCANDAL IN BOHEMIA

Sherlock Holmes is consulted by Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein about a scandal involving Irene Adler and a compromising photograph. He deduces details about the invitation note, identifies his visitor as the King of Bohemia, and agrees to try to recover the photograph.

II.

Sherlock Holmes spends the morning investigating Irene Adler and Briony Lodge while disguised as an unemployed groom. He gathers information from local horsemen, follows Adler and Godfrey Norton to the Church of St. Monica, unexpectedly witnesses their marriage, and later plans an operation at Briony Lodge with Dr. John Watson's assistance.

It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still

Sherlock Holmes directs the doctor to carry out a staged street disturbance and a false fire alarm designed to make Irene Adler reveal the photograph's hiding place. He pretends to be injured, is carried into Briony Lodge's sitting-room, and sees Adler reach behind a sliding panel above the right bell-pull. He plans to return with the King at eight the next morning, but postpones taking the photograph because the coachman is watching him.

III.

Sherlock Holmes returns to Briony Lodge with the King of Bohemia and learns that Irene Adler has left England. He finds her photograph and letter, realizes that she has outmaneuvered him, and asks the King to give him the photograph as his reward.

II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE

Sherlock Holmes questions Jabez Wilson about the Red-Headed League and asks him to repeat his story in detail for Dr. John Watson. He identifies facts about Wilson's background from his appearance, including manual labor, snuff-taking, Freemasonry, time in China, and recent writing.

Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful

Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. Jabez Wilson about the Red-headed League, its advertisement, and Vincent Spaulding. He inspects Saxe-Coburg Square, examines Spaulding’s trouser knees, and identifies Spaulding as a highly capable and daring man. Holmes believes a considerable crime is in contemplation and asks Dr. John Watson to help stop it that night.

It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way

Sherlock Holmes organizes the ambush in the bank cellar and captures John Clay when he emerges from the tunnel. He explains that the Red-headed League scheme was designed to keep Jabez Wilson away from his shop so Clay’s accomplice could dig toward the bank. He concludes that the tunnel was complete and predicts the robbery attempt for Saturday night.

III. A CASE OF IDENTITY

Sherlock Holmes receives Mary Sutherland as a client and infers details about her short sight and typewriting. He listens to her account of Mr. Hosmer Angel's disappearance, advises her to let the matter become a sealed book, and takes her letters and other papers to investigate.

Sherlock Holmes sat silent for a few minutes with his fingertips still

Sherlock Holmes examines Miss Mary Sutherland's clothing and physical details, including her sleeves, gloves, boots, and pince-nez marks, to infer that she is a typewriter user who left home in haste. He compares the typewritten letters from Hosmer Angel with James Windibank's writing, identifies matching defects in the typewriter, confronts Windibank, and explains how Windibank carried out the deception.

IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY

Sherlock Holmes is asked to investigate the Boscombe Valley tragedy after Inspector Lestrade becomes puzzled. He reviews the reported facts, questions the apparent strength of the case against James McCarthy, and intends to investigate personally while initially assuming that James’s account is true.

It was nearly four o’clock when we at last, after passing through the

Sherlock Holmes travels to Ross with Dr. Watson and Lestrade, initially preferring to remain at the hotel because of the high barometric pressure and good weather. After speaking with Miss Turner and visiting James McCarthy in prison, he becomes confident that James can be cleared and focuses on Mr. McCarthy's appointment at the pool and his cry of “Cooee!”

There was no rain, as Holmes had foretold, and the morning broke bright

Sherlock Holmes examines the boots, tracks, ground, trees, tobacco ash, and a stone near Boscombe Pool. He deduces the murderer’s physical characteristics and concludes that the criminal is John Turner.

The man who entered was a strange and impressive figure. His slow,

Sherlock Holmes summons old Turner privately, records his confession, and has Turner sign it with Watson as witness. He prepares objections for the defense, helping secure James McCarthy's acquittal, and keeps Turner's confession secret because it is no longer needed.

V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

Sherlock Holmes receives John Openshaw at Baker Street and listens to his account of the threats against the Openshaw family. He urges John to act immediately, criticizes the police for treating the warnings as practical jokes, and examines the surviving blue-tinted diary page.

“Thank you!” said Holmes, folding up the paper and returning it to our

Sherlock Holmes advises John Openshaw to put the remaining paper and a note in the brass box and place it on the sundial. After learning of John's death, Holmes investigates the case, traces the perpetrators to the Lone Star, and sends Captain James Calhoun five orange pips as a warning. He is deeply distressed that his advice sent John into danger and resolves to pursue the gang.

VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP

Sherlock Holmes is disguised as a decrepit old man in the opium den, where he is listening for clues while investigating Neville St. Clair's disappearance. He reveals himself to Watson, sends Isa home, and takes Watson to The Cedars to discuss the case.

“Mrs. St. Clair had fainted at the sight of the blood upon the window,

Sherlock Holmes investigates Neville St. Clair's disappearance with Dr. Watson and questions Mrs. St. Clair at The Cedars. He examines the letter, infers details about its envelope and posting, and considers both Neville's survival and the possibility of a forgery. He plans further inquiries for the following day.

A large and comfortable double-bedded room had been placed at our

Sherlock Holmes spends the night analyzing the case, then takes Watson to Bow Street to test his theory. He reveals that Hugh Boone is Neville St. Clair by removing Boone's disguise, and explains that he solved the matter through prolonged thought and observation.

VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE

Sherlock Holmes examines the battered black felt hat and deduces details about its unknown owner, including his intellect, former prosperity, declining circumstances, age, habits, and domestic situation. After Peterson finds the blue carbuncle in the Christmas goose, Holmes connects it to the Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery and advertises for Henry Baker so he can investigate further.

I had been delayed at a case, and it was a little after half-past six

Sherlock Holmes greets Henry Baker and returns his hat and a replacement goose. He explains that Baker's original goose was eaten and asks where it came from.

“So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door

Sherlock Holmes follows the goose supply chain from the Alpha Inn to Covent Garden Market and uses a wager to obtain Mr. Breckinridge’s records. He identifies James Ryder, obtains his confession, and releases him rather than sending him to the police, reasoning that this may save Ryder from a life of crime.

VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND

Sherlock Holmes receives Helen Stoner at Baker Street and questions her closely about her sister's death, the whistle, the bedroom, and the circumstances at Stoke Moran. He identifies mud and a return ticket as evidence of Helen's journey, notices five livid finger marks on her wrist, accuses her of screening her stepfather, and agrees to investigate the manor with Dr. Watson.

“And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,

Sherlock Holmes considers the nocturnal whistles, the gipsies, Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s financial interest, the dying woman’s words, and the metallic clang as possible clues. He confronts Roylott’s threats calmly, investigates the will of the deceased wife, examines Stoke Moran mansion, and concludes that Helen Stoner’s life may be in danger. He orders Helen to signal him after Roylott retires so that he and Watson can investigate her room during the night.

Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty in engaging a bedroom and

Sherlock Holmes deduces that the ventilator, dummy bell-rope, and clamped bed form a route for a snake to reach the bed. During the vigil, he attacks the snake with his cane, causing it to turn on Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and afterward explains how he reconstructed the murder scheme.

IX. THE ADVENTURE OF THE ENGINEER’S THUMB

Sherlock Holmes receives Watson and Hatherley at his Baker Street rooms, gives Hatherley food, brandy, and a place to rest, and listens as Hatherley begins recounting his strange experience.

We both sat in silence for some little time after listening to this

Sherlock Holmes identifies an advertisement for the disappearance of Jeremiah Hayling as evidence of the colonel's earlier use of the hydraulic machine. He deduces that the gang is operating near the centre of a ten-mile circle around Eyford and identifies them as large-scale coiners. At the fire, he concludes that the engineer's crushed oil-lamp caused the blaze and later explains how the engineer was carried from the garden.

X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR

Sherlock Holmes receives a letter from Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon requesting his judgment and discretion concerning the events surrounding the wedding. He reviews newspaper reports with Dr. John Watson and begins preparing to investigate Hatty Doran's disappearance.

“Lord Robert St. Simon,” announced our page-boy, throwing open the

Sherlock Holmes questions Lord Robert St. Simon closely about Hatty Doran, the wedding, Alice, and Flora Millar. He says that he has solved the case, having formed his conclusions before the interview and then confirmed them through the evidence.

The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which

Sherlock Holmes quickly concludes that Lady St. Simon is not dead and eventually reveals that she is a myth under that name. He deduces that she saw an American from her past at the wedding, identifies Francis Hay Moulton through the initials and hotel-bill fragment, finds the couple at 226 Gordon Square, and brings them before Lord St. Simon.

XI. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BERYL CORONET

Sherlock Holmes receives Alexander Holder at Baker Street and calms him after Holder arrives in extreme distress. He listens to Holder's detailed account of the coronet, the loan, and the events at Holder's house.

Sherlock Holmes sat silent for some few minutes, with his brows knitted

Sherlock Holmes sits silent for some few minutes with his brows knitted. He keeps his eyes fixed upon the fire.

“Do you receive much company?” he asked.

Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. Holder and Mary Holder, inspects Fairbank and the coronet, and notices that breaking off the missing section would require great force and make a loud noise. He investigates in disguise, recovers the three stolen gems, and tells Mr. Holder that Arthur Holder is innocent.

“For Heaven’s sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary mystery!”

Sherlock Holmes reconstructs the coronet theft from footprints, blood, window marks, and other evidence. He disguises himself as a loafer, identifies Sir George Burnwell through his valet and cast-off shoes, confronts him, and recovers the missing gems without a prosecution.

XII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE COPPER BEECHES

Sherlock Holmes receives Violet Hunter at Baker Street and examines her account of the governess position at the Copper Beeches. He considers the high salary and unusual conditions suspicious, warns that the household may be dangerous, and promises to help if she sends a telegram. When her telegram arrives, he postpones his chemical research and plans to travel with Dr. John Watson to Winchester.

By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old

Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. Watson to Winchester to investigate Miss Hunter's appeal for help. He listens closely to her account and says that he has devised seven possible explanations for the facts known so far.

“‘So,’ said he, smiling, ‘it was you, then. I thought that it must be

Mr. Holmes is the person whom the young lady contacts for help and advice about the household. She comes to Winchester hoping that his assistance will make the situation better.

Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My

Sherlock Holmes arranges with Violet Hunter to investigate the Copper Beeches after the Rucastles leave, asking her to lock Mrs. Toller in the cellar. He deduces that Violet was brought there to impersonate Alice Rucastle and that Alice was imprisoned in the chamber. Holmes confronts Mr. Rucastle, helps expose the escape route, and later recognizes that Mrs. Toller’s account explains the remaining mystery.

Sherlock Holmes in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle · about 1892 to 1893 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a London consulting detective, reasoner, and unofficial investigator who lives at Baker Street, works by observation, deduction, physical evidence, and analytical reasoning, and is chron­icled and frequently accompanied by his friend Dr. John Watson. He has remarkable detective gifts, medical knowledge of ears, expertise in chemical research, skill as a boxer, and habits marked by austere living, violin playing, occasional cocaine use when cases are scarce, and avoidance of unnecessary exertion. He loves London but has little attraction to nature, and he is generally disinclined to new friendships and averse to women. Across investigations in town and country, Holmes repeatedly separates fact from speculation and reconstructs crimes from small clues. At King’s Pyland, he recovers Silver Blaze and determines that John Straker died when the horse defended itself. He identifies Jim Browner as the killer connected to the packet of ears, investigates the cottage mystery and learns not to be overconfident, exposes the fraud involving Hall Pycroft’s handwriting, and recounts early cases involving the Gloria Scott cipher and the Musgrave Ritual’s concealed chamber. While recovering from exhaustion, he solves William Kirwan’s murder and exposes the Cunninghams. He investigates Colonel Barclay’s death, Blessington’s murder, the abduction of Paul Kratides, and the theft of Percy Phelps’s treaty, recovering the stolen State papers from Joseph Harrison. Holmes regards his methods as open to Watson and other interested observers, while Watson regards him as the best and wisest man he has known. Holmes says he has solved over a thousand cases and used his powers on the side of the law without known exception. The account culminates in his years-long effort against Professor Moriarty, his approximate intellectual equal and leader of a hidden criminal organization. Pursued and attacked by Moriarty’s agents, Holmes evades surveillance with Watson across Europe, ensures evidence against the gang will be found, and confronts Moriarty at Reichenbach Falls. After leaving Watson a farewell note, Holmes dies with Moriarty after their personal contest there.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

34 sections; each heading opens the text

I. Silver Blaze

Sherlock Holmes decides to travel to Dartmoor and King’s Pyland with John Watson to investigate the case. He separates established facts from speculation, identifies weaknesses in the police theory, and plans to examine the evidence at the scene.

It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock,

Sherlock Holmes questions Inspector Gregory, examines Straker’s possessions and the crime scene, and finds a burned wax vesta and tracks leading toward Mapleton. He reasons that Silver Blaze must be at Mapleton, confronts Silas Brown, and secures the horse’s safety, but leaves the investigation of John Straker’s killer unresolved.

“My friend and I return to town by the night-express,” said

Sherlock Holmes says that there are grave difficulties in arresting the murderer of John Straker, but he expects the horse to start on Tuesday. He obtains a photograph of John Straker, questions the maid, notices the lameness among the sheep, and points Inspector Gregory toward the dog's inactivity at night.

Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for

Sherlock Holmes identifies the disguised bay horse as Silver Blaze and reveals that John Straker was killed by the horse in self-defence. He reconstructs the crime from the curried mutton, the silent stable dog, Straker's surgical knife, his bills, and the horse's behaviour, and later finds the recovered horse with a neighbour.

II. The Adventure of the Cardboard Box

Sherlock Holmes reads Watson’s train of thought from his facial expressions, eyes, gestures, and other movements, then explains each deduction. He brings Watson’s attention to a newspaper report about a packet sent to Miss Cushing and identifies it as a potentially difficult problem.

I picked up the paper which he had thrown back to me and read the

Sherlock Holmes examines the packet, its tarred twine, wrapper, box, salt, and the two ears. He concludes that the ears came from a woman and a man who were probably murdered, connects the case to Mary Cushing’s husband James Browner, and gives Inspector Lestrade the suspected criminal’s name.

“The case,” said Sherlock Holmes as we chatted over our cigars

Sherlock Holmes reasons backward from the evidence and identifies the sailor-related clues in the little yellow box. He matches one ear in the box to Miss Cushing’s ear, learns about the Cushing sisters and Jim Browner, and concludes that Browner probably committed the murders from jealousy.

Sherlock Holmes was not disappointed in his expectations. Two

Sherlock Holmes receives Inspector Lestrade's report and reads James Browner's statement aloud to Watson. He considers the investigation simple in retrospect but ends by questioning what purpose is served by the cycle of misery, violence, and fear.

III. The Yellow Face

Sherlock Holmes receives Grant Munro at Baker Street and agrees to hear his domestic problem. Before Grant explains the case, Holmes examines a pipe left behind by the earlier visitor and deduces that its owner is muscular, left-handed, well-to-do, careless, and has strong teeth.

“For two days after this I stayed at home, and my wife appeared

Sherlock Holmes investigates the cottage mystery and initially theorizes that Effie’s first husband or his associates are blackmailing her. He discovers that the livid face belongs to a masked child and later admits that the case should remind him not to become overconfident.

IV. The Stockbroker’s Clerk

Sherlock Holmes deduces from Watson’s scorched slippers that Watson recently had a severe chill. He takes Watson to Birmingham to investigate Hall Pycroft’s case and recognizes that the two supposed Pinner brothers are the same man because they share the same voice, figure, and identically stuffed tooth.

There was a pause after the stockbroker’s clerk had concluded his

Sherlock Holmes visits Arthur Harry Pinner with Dr. John Watson and Hall Pycroft, questions the circumstances, and breaks into the inner room when Pinner begins choking himself. He deduces that Pycroft’s handwriting was obtained for imitation and that one of the criminals impersonated Pycroft at Mawson & Williams; he later recognizes the Evening Standard report as explaining Pinner’s suicide attempt.

V. The “_Gloria Scott_”

Sherlock Holmes recounts his first criminal case to Dr. Watson. During his visit to Donnithorpe, he deduces details about Mr. Trevor's past from his appearance and later recognizes that the strange message contains a hidden meaning.

“It was short and terse, the warning, as I now read it to my

Holmes explains how the warning message's prearranged cipher works and infers that its sporting vocabulary suggests the sender is an ardent shot or interested in breeding. He asks Victor whether he knows anything about Beddoes and concludes that Beddoes sent the note.

VI. The Musgrave Ritual

Sherlock Holmes recounts the Musgrave Ritual case to Dr. John Watson. He is consulted by Reginald Musgrave after Brunton and Rachel Howells disappear, and he begins investigating by asking to see the ritual document.

“The same afternoon saw us both at Hurlstone. Possibly you have

Sherlock Holmes interprets the Musgrave Ritual, uses the oak, the former elm, the sun, and the stated measurements to locate the concealed cellar chamber, and finds Brunton’s body there. He reconstructs Brunton’s investigation and probable death, identifies the recovered relic as the ancient crown of the Kings of England, and explains its historical significance to Reginald Musgrave.

VII. The Reigate Squires

Sherlock Holmes visits Reigate with Dr. Watson while recovering from the strain of a prolonged investigation. Although he initially agrees to rest, he becomes intensely interested in the Acton burglary and the Cunningham burglary and murder, examines the fragment of paper, visits the crime scene with Inspector Forrester, and develops theories about William Kirwan's letter and the missing portion of the note.

We passed the pretty cottage where the murdered man had lived,

Sherlock Holmes examines the Cunningham house and questions the family about the burglary, the house’s layout, and the events surrounding William Kirwan’s death. He pretends to suffer nervous attacks, deliberately knocks over a dish of oranges and water, and uses the confusion to search for evidence. After being attacked by the Cunninghams, he orders their arrest and produces the remainder of a sheet of paper as evidence.

Sherlock Holmes was as good as his word, for about one o’clock he

Sherlock Holmes explains his deductions about the note, the original burglary, and the killing of William Kirwan. He determines that the Cunninghams were responsible, recovers the missing part of the note, and obtains Cunningham's confession.

VIII. The Crooked Man

Sherlock Holmes visits Watson at nearly midnight and deduces details about Watson's work and habits from his appearance and surroundings. He asks Watson to travel with him to Aldershot and outlines his investigation into the supposed murder of Colonel Barclay, saying that he is close to solving it but lacks one or two necessary facts.

“Mrs. Barclay was, it appears, a member of the Roman Catholic

Sherlock Holmes investigates Colonel Barclay’s death at Major Murphy’s request. He examines the room, lawn, footprints, missing key, and animal traces, then questions Miss Morrison and searches for Henry Wood. Holmes concludes that Wood followed the women, entered through the window with the strange animal, and may be able to explain the death.

It was midday when we found ourselves at the scene of the

Sherlock Holmes visits Henry Wood with Watson to investigate Colonel James Barclay's death and determine whether Nancy Barclay is in danger of being tried for murder. He learns Wood's account of James Barclay's betrayal and concludes that the inquest's finding of apoplexy makes further investigation unnecessary.

IX. The Resident Patient

Holmes listens to Dr. Percy Trevelyan's account of Blessington's fears, the supposed Russian patients, and the footprints in Blessington's room. He accompanies Trevelyan and Watson to Brook Street, questions Blessington about the two men, and concludes that Blessington is not telling the truth.

A minute later we were in the street and walking for home. We had

Holmes deduces that the catalepsy was a fraudulent imitation and that at least two men were pursuing Blessington. After examining the bedroom, cigar ends, footprints, lock, rope, and other traces, he determines that Blessington was murdered by three men and identifies Blessington as Sutton, a former member of the Worthingdon bank gang.

X. The Greek Interpreter

Sherlock Holmes explains to John Watson that his older brother Mycroft Holmes has greater powers of observation and deduction than he does, although Mycroft lacks ambition and energy for practical detective work. He visits the Diogenes Club with John Watson and listens to Mr. Melas recount the abduction and interrogation of Kratides.

“I cannot tell you the loathing and horror with which this

Sherlock Holmes concludes that Paul Kratides is in immediate danger and takes up the case. He telegraphs for information, brings Mycroft Holmes and Dr. Watson to Scotland Yard and Beckenham, deduces that a heavily loaded carriage has left The Myrtles, enters through an open window, and rescues Mr. Melas and Paul from the poisoned room. He later believes that Sophy Kratides may have avenged herself and her brother on Harold Latimer and Wilson Kemp.

XI. The Naval Treaty

Sherlock Holmes agrees to accompany Dr. John Watson to Woking after reading Percy Phelps's letter. He observes that the letter was written by a woman of unusual character, questions Phelps closely about the treaty theft, and identifies several important details, including the quarter-to-ten time and the absence of muddy footprints.

“We examined the room also. There is no possibility of a secret

Sherlock Holmes questions Phelps closely about who knew of the special task, the commissionnaire, and the circumstances of the theft. He identifies several possible clues, advertises for the number of a cab at the Foreign Office, and begins by consulting Mr. Forbes at Scotland Yard.

“Where are we going to now?” I asked, as we left the office.

Sherlock Holmes questions Lord Holdhurst about the copying of the naval treaty and reasons that the thief may not have delivered it to a foreign government. In Woking, he examines the alleged intrusion, notices that the evidence is inconclusive, orders Annie Harrison to remain in Phelps's room and lock it from the outside, and sends Phelps and Dr. John Watson to London while he stays behind to investigate.

It was seven o’clock when I awoke, and I set off at once for

Sherlock Holmes spends the night watching Percy Phelps’s room at Briarbrae after arranging for Miss Harrison to lock the door and take its key. He intercepts Joseph Harrison as Joseph retrieves the stolen papers, overcomes him after suffering a cut to the hand, and returns the papers to Phelps. Holmes explains that Joseph’s actions and the earlier events form the solution to the case.

XII. The Final Problem

Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. John Watson that he has spent years tracing the hidden organization behind numerous crimes and has identified Professor Moriarty as its leader. He has nearly completed his investigation and plans to withdraw temporarily so that the police can arrest Moriarty and the principal members of his gang. Holmes has survived several attacks, including an attempted vehicular assault, a falling brick, and an attack by a man with a bludgeon.

In the morning I obeyed Holmes’s injunctions to the letter. A

Holmes arranges Watson’s journey and reserves a carriage for him. He reaches the train disguised as an aged Italian priest, reveals himself just before departure, warns Watson that pursuit is continuing, and then removes and packs away his disguise.

“Have you seen the morning paper, Watson?”

Holmes learns that the rooms at Baker Street were set on fire and concludes that Moriarty has been watching Watson. He arranges an evasive escape journey, predicts Moriarty's movements, and avoids him at Canterbury.

We made our way to Brussels that night and spent two days there,

Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. John Watson through Switzerland while remaining alert to Professor Moriarty's pursuit. He confronts Moriarty at Reichenbach Falls and is presumed to have fallen into the chasm with him. In his farewell note, he states that he deliberately allowed Watson to leave and had arranged for evidence against Moriarty's gang to be found.

Sherlock Holmes in The Hound of the Baskervilles

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1901 to 1902 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is the central figure of the Baskerville adventure: a London-based consulting detective, specialist in crime and scientific deduction, and friend and companion of Dr. John Watson. Clear, alert, professionally cautious, and able to detach his mind at will, he uses close observation, maps, printed matter, portraits, reports, and concealed surveillance to investigate Sir Charles Baskerville’s death and protect Sir Henry Baskerville. He begins by deducing facts from Dr. James Mortimer’s stick, dating and assessing a manuscript, questioning Mortimer about the death, and examining the warning letter. His inquiries identify surveillance of Sir Henry, but several London leads fail, so he sends Watson to Devonshire with strict instructions to report facts, stay with Sir Henry, and keep him from the moor alone. Although occupied by other cases, Holmes secretly travels to the moor, lives in a hut with Cartwright’s help, receives Watson’s delayed reports, and investigates from Coombe Tracey. He identifies Miss Stapleton as Jack Stapleton’s wife, recognizes Stapleton as the enemy and a Baskerville through a portrait, and concludes that Sir Charles died of fright caused by a hound. Refusing to arrest Stapleton on conjecture, Holmes gathers proof through Mrs. Laura Lyons and arranges a trap using Sir Henry. During the ambush he shoots the hound, rescues Sir Henry, finds Mrs. Stapleton, and follows Stapleton’s route into the Grimpen Mire, where he explains the missing boot, the hound’s confinement and luminous coating, and Stapleton’s deception. He ends by reconstructing the mystery from testimony and notes, having exposed the deliberate plot against Sir Henry.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

20 sections; each heading opens the text

The Hound of the Baskervilles

Sherlock Holmes is identified as the central figure of this adventure. The contents name him in the opening chapter, "Mr. Sherlock Holmes."

Chapter 1.

Mr. Sherlock Holmes examines Dr. James Mortimer’s presentation stick and uses its markings and wear to reconstruct details about its owner. He correctly infers that Mortimer is a country practitioner who walks a great deal, identifies “C.C.H.” as Charing Cross Hospital, and recognizes tooth marks from a curly-haired spaniel. He invites Mortimer to explain the serious problem that has brought him to seek assistance.

Chapter 2.

Sherlock Holmes dates the manuscript to the early eighteenth century by examining its script and reads the public account of Sir Charles Baskerville's death. After initially dismissing the legend as a fairy tale, he asks Dr. James Mortimer to provide the private facts of the case.

Chapter 3.

Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Mortimer closely about the footprints, the yew alley, the moor-gate, and Sir Charles Baskerville's final movements. He studies a map of Dartmoor, considers natural explanations before supernatural ones, and concludes that Sir Charles was running for his life. Holmes advises Mortimer to meet Sir Henry Baskerville at Waterloo Station and to tell him nothing until Holmes has made up his mind.

Chapter 4.

Sherlock Holmes examines Sir Henry Baskerville’s warning letter and identifies its words as having been cut from a Times leading article. He infers that the sender was educated, attempted to disguise his handwriting, used nail-scissors and gum, and probably composed the message in a hotel near Charing Cross. He discusses the possible danger of Sir Henry going to Baskerville Hall and agrees to meet him and Dr. Watson for lunch.

We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang

Holmes changes quickly from a languid dreamer into a man of action and follows Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville with Watson. He recognizes that a cab is following them, but his eagerness to pursue it betrays him and allows the unknown man to escape. Holmes records the cab number as 2704, sends Cartwright to search hotel waste-paper, and plans to identify the cabman by wire.

Chapter 5.

Sherlock Holmes examines the Northumberland Hotel register, investigates the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, and questions the financial circumstances surrounding Sir Charles Baskerville's will and estate. He arranges telegrams to verify Barrymore's whereabouts, recruits Dr. Watson to accompany Sir Henry, and questions John Clayton about the black-bearded spy. Holmes concludes that three investigative leads have failed in London and becomes concerned about sending Watson to Devonshire.

Chapter 6.

Sherlock Holmes accompanies Dr. Watson to the station and instructs him to report facts rather than theories. He says that James Desmond can probably be eliminated from consideration, but that the Barrymore couple and the other people around Sir Henry must remain under suspicion. Holmes also warns Sir Henry not to go about alone, to keep his revolver near him, and to avoid the moor at night.

Chapter 7.

Sherlock Holmes has sent Dr. Watson to investigate the neighbors and has arranged a test telegram intended to determine whether Barrymore was in London. Watson hopes Holmes will soon be free to take responsibility for the case, but Holmes cannot leave town because of other cases.

Chapter 8.

Mr. Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s letters and telegrams about events at Baskerville Hall. He had instructed Watson never to allow Sir Henry Baskerville to go out alone and asked him to provide factual reports about the people around them.

Chapter 9.

Sherlock Holmes had instructed Dr. Watson not to leave Sir Henry Baskerville, especially not to let him go alone upon the moor. Watson tries to follow those instructions despite Sir Henry’s objections.

So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is

Sherlock Holmes is the intended recipient of Dr. Watson’s report and had sent Watson to investigate the case. Watson asks him to judge the progress of the investigation.

Chapter 10.

Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s reports from the moor, including the information about the woman identified by the initials L. L. Watson expects this new clue to renew Holmes’s interest and perhaps bring him to Devonshire.

Chapter 12.

Sherlock Holmes has been secretly living in a hut on the moor with assistance from Cartwright while investigating the case. He tells Dr. John Watson that Miss Stapleton is Jack Stapleton’s wife, identifies Stapleton as their enemy, and says that the murder plot is deliberate and directed against Sir Henry Baskerville.

A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst

Sherlock Holmes runs across the moor with Dr. John Watson after hearing screams and initially believes Sir Henry Baskerville has been killed. He is relieved to discover that the victim is Selden, then reasons that the hound was drawn by Sir Henry’s clothing. Holmes conceals his suspicions from Stapleton and says that the investigation has not been satisfactory.

“We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together

Sherlock Holmes believes the criminal is an exceptionally worthy opponent and may respond to being discovered by becoming more cautious or taking desperate measures. He refuses to arrest him without proof and plans to use Mrs. Laura Lyons and his own investigation to establish a case. He tells Dr. Watson to conceal the hound from Sir Henry and to excuse himself from the planned dinner.

Chapter 13.

Sherlock Holmes recognizes a resemblance between Mr. Stapleton and the portrait of Hugo Baskerville, concluding that Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs upon the succession. He secretly arranges a trap involving Sir Henry, visits Mrs. Laura Lyons to obtain her testimony, and summons Inspector Lestrade with an unsigned warrant.

Chapter 14.

Sherlock Holmes leads the ambush near Merripit House and keeps his plans secret until the action begins. He shoots the hound, rescues Sir Henry, finds Mrs. Stapleton, and learns that Stapleton may be hiding in the Grimpen Mire.

And now I come rapidly to the conclusion of this singular

Holmes follows the marked path through the Grimpen Mire with Watson and others, nearly sinking when he leaves the path to retrieve a dark object. He identifies the object as Sir Henry’s missing boot and explains that Stapleton carried and discarded it while fleeing. Holmes also identifies the hound’s confinement, its luminous coating, and the purpose of Stapleton’s deception.

Chapter 15.

Sherlock Holmes reconstructs the Baskerville mystery after speaking with Mrs. Stapleton and reviewing his notes. He secretly went to Devonshire, watched Stapleton, used Cartwright for assistance, and helped use Sir Henry as bait to expose the plot.

Sherlock Holmes in The Return of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1903-09-26 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a living, six-foot-tall criminal investigator, detective, consulting detective, and criminal expert, based at and repeatedly returning to Baker Street, where he resides and works with his close friend, colleague, partner, and companion Dr. John Watson. He is famed for peculiar powers of deduction, uses deductive and inductive reasoning, studies physical traces, codes, maps, documents, and human conduct, and applies intense effort especially to strange, dramatic, or sympathetic cases rather than seeking large rewards or official position. After surviving the Reichenbach Fall and Professor Moriarty, Holmes spends nearly three years hidden, travelling in Tibet under the alias Sigerson, researching at Montpellier, visiting Khartoum, and concealing himself through disguises. He returns as an old book collector, learns an enemy remains in London, and uses a wax bust decoy to expose and secure the arrest of Colonel Sebastian Moran, whom he identifies as Ronald Adair’s murderer. With Moran removed, he is free to examine London again. His subsequent work unfolds through varied investigations with Watson and police contacts including Lestrade, Hopkins, and Martin. He exposes Jonas Oldacre’s staged death in the Norwood builder case; deciphers the dancing-men cipher, clears Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, and traps Abe Slaney; protects Violet Smith from an abduction and forced-marriage scheme; and resolves Lord Saltire’s disappearance by following bicycle tracks, recognizing a false cow-track trail, and confronting the Duke of Holdernesse. He also investigates Peter Carey’s death, attempts the recovery of blackmail letters from Charles Augustus Milverton, recovers the black pearl of the Borgias from a bust, identifies Gilchrist in the examination-paper theft, and investigates Willoughby Smith’s murder at Yoxley Old Place. Holmes’s methods include aliases such as Captain Basil and Escott, cultivated night vision, boxing, baritsu, revolvers when danger is expected, ciphers, and occasional burglary tools. He plays violin to soothe himself, smokes heavily, may forgo food during intense work, and keeps extensive biographical and other investigative materials. His work is marked by discretion, independence, readiness to confront danger, and a strong personal bond with Watson.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

28 sections; each heading opens the text

THE ADVENTURE OF THE EMPTY HOUSE

Sherlock Holmes reveals himself to Dr. John Watson in disguise as an elderly book collector. He explains that he survived the Reichenbach Fall, spent nearly three years concealing his identity and travelling abroad, and returned to London to deal with his remaining enemy and investigate the Park Lane Mystery.

Such was the remarkable narrative to which I listened on that

Sherlock Holmes returns to London after three years and secretly arranges a trap for Colonel Sebastian Moran. He and Dr. John Watson watch a wax bust of him in the Baker Street rooms from Camden House, then overpower Moran after Moran fires at the bust. Holmes identifies Moran as the killer of the Honourable Ronald Adair and gives Inspector Lestrade credit for the arrest.

Our old chambers had been left unchanged through the supervision

Sherlock Holmes returns to his old chambers, uses a wax dummy dressed in his clothing to draw Colonel Sebastian Moran's fire, and has Moran arrested. He explains Moran's criminal history to Dr. John Watson and theorizes that Moran murdered the Honourable Ronald Adair after Adair discovered his card cheating.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE NORWOOD BUILDER

Mr. Sherlock Holmes discusses the decline of sensational criminal cases in London and receives John Hector McFarlane as a client. He identifies McFarlane as a bachelor, solicitor, Freemason, and asthmatic, reads the newspaper report, and begins investigating the suspected murder of Jonas Oldacre.

It was a clang of the bell, followed instantly by heavy steps

Sherlock Holmes questions McFarlane about the house, the window, and the circumstances of his departure. He argues that the case is too obvious, observes that the rough draft of the will was written on a train, and proposes that a passing tramp may have killed Oldacre and burned the body.

When the detective departed, my friend rose and made his

Sherlock Holmes investigates Oldacre's apparent murder by visiting Blackheath and Deep Dene House, examining the physical evidence and questioning Mrs. Lexington. He recognizes that the newly discovered blood thumbprint is suspicious because it was absent when he inspected the hall, and he ultimately exposes Jonas Oldacre by creating a simulated fire and alarm.

Holmes smiled, and clapped Lestrade upon the shoulder.

Sherlock Holmes explains Oldacre’s hidden room, the origin of the thumb-mark, and the motive behind Oldacre’s deception. He tells Lestrade that Oldacre’s creditors may impound Mr. Cornelius’s bank account and questions Oldacre about the contents of the wood-pile.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN

Sherlock Holmes receives Hilton Cubitt's dancing-men messages and begins investigating their meaning. He asks Cubitt to gather further evidence, studies the figures intensively, sends a telegram for additional information, and concludes that the case is dangerous enough to require an immediate visit to Norfolk.

So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a

Sherlock Holmes travels to Riding Thorpe Manor with Dr. Watson, intending to prevent the threatened tragedy, but arrives after Hilton Cubitt has been killed and his wife has been seriously wounded. He examines the scene, identifies a third bullet and cartridge, reconstructs the likely presence of a person outside the window, and deciphers the dancing men messages. He sends a note to Abe Slaney at Elrige’s Farm and advises Inspector Martin to arrange an escort for Slaney.

“It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a

Sherlock Holmes writes a coded invitation to Abe Slaney, anticipates that Slaney will come, and directs Inspector Martin to arrest him. He explains the dancing-men cipher, establishes that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was not responsible for her husband's death, and uses Slaney's confession to clarify the case.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST

Sherlock Holmes interviews Violet Smith about the cyclist who follows her and deduces details about her bicycling, music teaching, and circumstances. He notices that the pursuer disappears near Charlington Hall, suspects a connection involving Mr. Carruthers and Mr. Woodley, and sends Watson to investigate.

We had ascertained from the lady that she went down upon the

Mr. Sherlock Holmes reviews Watson’s report and criticizes him for observing from too far away and for consulting a house agent rather than a local public-house. Holmes later investigates the area himself, learns more about Williamson and Mr. Woodley, and returns to Baker Street bruised after fighting Woodley.

The Thursday brought us another letter from our client.

Sherlock Holmes concludes that a serious intrigue surrounds Violet Smith and travels with Dr. Watson to protect her on her journey. He follows the abductors’ trail, confronts Williamson, takes control of the scene, and summons the police. He explains that Williamson’s authority to solemnize the marriage is doubtful, that the marriage was forced, and that the criminal scheme arose from Ralph Smith’s expected death and Violet’s inheritance.

Holmes rose and tossed the end of his cigarette into the grate.

Holmes concludes that the case has been solved and offers Mr. Carruthers his evidence for use at trial. He asks Watson to check whether Miss Violet Smith has recovered sufficiently to return to her mother’s home.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate the disappearance of Lord Saltire after learning of the five-thousand-pound reward for locating him and the additional reward for identifying his abductors. He questions Thorneycroft Huxtable, challenges the theory that Heidegger used the bicycle as a false clue, and travels with Dr. Watson to Mackleton. He also questions the Duke of Holdernesse about the Duchess, a possible ransom, and the letter sent to Lord Saltire.

When the nobleman and his secretary had left, my friend flung

Sherlock Holmes examines the school grounds, maps the surrounding area, questions the evidence about the roads, and searches the moor with Dr. Watson. He identifies Heidegger’s Palmer tire tracks, follows them to the German master’s body, and reasons that the boy left voluntarily with a companion who had another bicycle.

When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was

Sherlock Holmes realizes that the cow-tracks vary as though the animal walked, cantered, and galloped, concluding that they are a deliberate blind. He examines the horses and the Fighting Cock, observes James Wilder's secret activity, and sends telegrams from Mackleton Station before promising that the mystery will soon be solved.

At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up

Sherlock Holmes confronts the Duke of Holdernesse, identifies him as responsible for concealing Lord Saltire’s whereabouts, and demands the promised reward. He reveals that Reuben Hayes has been arrested, secures orders for Lord Saltire’s return, and agrees not to disclose everything he knows if justice is otherwise served.

THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER

Sherlock Holmes has been investigating the tragedy at Woodman's Lee under disguises and names, and he tests his ability to kill a pig with a barbed-headed spear. After hearing Stanley Hopkins's account and examining the evidence, he agrees to visit Peter Carey's cabin with Hopkins and Dr. Watson.

Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles

Sherlock Holmes examines the attempted forced entry, infers that the visitor will return with a stronger tool, and helps arrange the stakeout. He searches Captain Peter Carey's hut for evidence, notices that something has been removed from a shelf, and watches as John Hopley Neligan searches a logbook.

THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON

Sherlock Holmes negotiates with Charles Augustus Milverton on Lady Eva Blackwell’s behalf but cannot reduce the demand for the compromising letters. He disguises himself as a workman named Escott to gather information about Milverton’s house, then plans to burgle it with Dr. Watson.

Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to

Sherlock Holmes disguises himself with Dr. John Watson and breaks into Charles Milverton’s house to open the safe and destroy the blackmail documents. He hides from Milverton and restrains Watson from intervening when the unnamed woman shoots Milverton. Afterward, Holmes burns the documents, escapes with Watson, refuses Lestrade’s request to investigate, and recognizes the avenging woman from a photograph.

When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much

Sherlock Holmes purchases the Reading bust from Mr. Sandeford for ten pounds and has the seller transfer every possible right to it. He breaks the bust open and finds the famous black pearl of the Borgias, then explains how he traced it through the six busts and related crimes.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE STUDENTS

Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Hilton Soames’s confidential examination-paper case. He infers that the intruder moved the pages to the window table, copied at least part of them, broke and resharpened a large soft-leaded pencil, and then hid in Soames’s bedroom before escaping. He examines Bannister and the three students’ rooms, takes the black clay and pencil cuttings, and postpones his conclusion until the following morning.

When we were out in the darkness of the quadrangle, we again

Holmes discusses the three students with Watson and considers the Indian student's pacing unimportant because he may have been memorizing material. He is particularly puzzled by Bannister's behavior and investigates the pencil by visiting the town's four significant stationers.

Holmes made no further allusion to the matter that day, though he

Sherlock Holmes works through the night and early morning, obtains a third black clay sample from the athletic grounds, and concludes that he has solved the mystery. He identifies Gilchrist as the culprit, reconstructs the attempted theft and hiding place, and explains Bannister’s actions.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE GOLDEN PINCE-NEZ

Sherlock Holmes hears Stanley Hopkins's account of the Yoxley Old Place murder and examines the evidence. He studies the golden pince-nez, makes deductions about its owner, and agrees to investigate the case at Yoxley Old Place.

The gale had blown itself out next day, but it was a bitter

Sherlock Holmes examines the garden path, the study, the wooden bureau, and the professor’s room while reconstructing the events surrounding Willoughby Smith’s death. He questions Professor Coram and Mrs. Marker, smokes several Alexandrian cigarettes as part of a possible test, and plans to confront Professor Coram at two o’clock.

Sherlock Holmes in The Return of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1903-09-26 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a private, consulting detective and specialist investigator based at Baker Street, with Dr. John Watson as companion, friend, colleague, and frequent investigative partner. He has vast knowledge, forensic skill, and expertise across many sections of society; works as an irregular pioneer ahead of official forces; keeps contact with Scotland Yard; and values discretion, cautioning against action on incomplete evidence. He sometimes works as an agent, uses aliases and investigative tools, and plans to write a textbook in his declining years before retiring to the Sussex Downs. Across these records, Holmes solves or advances several investigations through close physical clues, records, interviews, traps, and deductions. In Peter Carey’s killing, he rejects the case against young Neligan, infers a powerful practiced seaman from the harpoon, traces Sea Unicorn crew records to Patrick Cairns, and lures Cairns to Baker Street as Captain Basil, recommending Neligan’s release. In the Napoleon bust destruction series, he traces the busts to their source, anticipates an attack on the remaining busts, and helps arrest Beppo. He also identifies Anna’s hidden presence in Professor Coram’s house through the pince-nez, food use, and cigarette ash. Holmes investigates Godfrey Staunton’s disappearance by tracing Dr. Leslie Armstrong’s carriage with aniseed and Pompey, finding Staunton and his dead wife, then protecting the private matter from publicity. At Abbey Grange, he exposes the false burglary account, identifies Captain Crocker as responsible for the killing, and informally acquits him after judging the act potentially self-defense under extreme provocation. Finally, while investigating Eduardo Lucas’s murder and its link to the Whitehall Terrace incident, Holmes focuses on recovering a missing political document to prevent a European catastrophe. He uncovers Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope’s role, obtains the document, and restores it to the despatch-box without revealing its location.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

14 sections; each heading opens the text

“Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we

Sherlock Holmes rejects Hopkins’s explanation of Peter Carey’s killing because young Neligan could not have delivered the immensely powerful harpoon blow. He traces the clues to a seaman who served on the Sea Unicorn, identifies Patrick Cairns among its 1883 harpooners, and lures Cairns to Baker Street by advertising an Arctic expedition under the name Captain Basil. Holmes handcuffs Cairns and explains that the evidence points to him as the true killer, while advising Hopkins to release young Neligan.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS

Sherlock Holmes listens to Inspector Lestrade's account of the Napoleon bust destruction series and identifies a method in the image-breaker's actions. He examines the Pitt Street scene, the bust fragments, and the photograph found on the dead man, while suggesting that the busts have greater significance than their apparent value.

Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where

Sherlock Holmes investigates the source and destruction of the Napoleon busts, tracing them through Morse Hudson, Harding Brothers, and Gelder & Co. He uses the evening newspaper and a letter to Josiah Brown to lure Beppo into attacking the remaining bust at Laburnum Villa, where he helps arrest him. Holmes examines the broken bust and says that important details of the case remain unresolved.

The old man had just finished his lunch, and certainly his empty

Sherlock Holmes solves the case by deducing that Anna remained inside Professor Coram’s house after the murder. He identifies the hidden bookcase room, exposes Coram’s role in concealing Anna, receives the packet for Alexis, and explains how the pince-nez, increased food consumption, and cigarette ash led to his solution.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE MISSING THREE-QUARTER

Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Godfrey Staunton’s disappearance after Cyril Overton is referred to him by Scotland Yard. He questions the hotel porter, examines Staunton’s papers and blotting-paper, obtains the telegram’s final words, and travels toward Cambridge with Dr. John Watson.

It was already dark when we reached the old university city.

Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Leslie Armstrong about Godfrey Staunton and presents evidence linking Armstrong to Staunton. After being expelled, he investigates Armstrong's carriage journeys by questioning people and following the carriage by bicycle, but he loses track of it. He concludes that Armstrong knows where Staunton is and plans to continue investigating.

And yet the next day brought us no nearer to the solution of the

Holmes investigates Dr. Armstrong’s movements and uses a syringe of aniseed on the doctor’s carriage wheel so that Pompey can follow the trail. He reaches the lonely cottage with Watson, discovers Godfrey Staunton and his dead wife, and promises Dr. Armstrong to keep the private matter out of the papers.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE ABBEY GRANGE

Sherlock Holmes travels with Dr. John Watson to Abbey Grange after receiving Inspector Stanley Hopkins’s urgent summons. He initially believes the case concerns a murder and examines Lady Brackenstall, the dining-room, the bindings, the French window, the poker, and the three wine glasses, noticing details that challenge the apparent simplicity of the burglary.

A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless

Sherlock Holmes examines the cork, wine glasses, bell-rope, bracket, chair, window, curtains, carpet, and rope at the Abbey Grange. He concludes that Lady Brackenstall’s story is fabricated, that one unusually strong and agile man was involved, and that the evidence points toward someone connected with her past. He investigates Miss Fraser’s voyage and Jack Crocker’s record, sends a telegram, and delays seeking a warrant because he fears causing unjust harm.

Dinner was over, and the table cleared before Holmes alluded to

Sherlock Holmes summons Captain Crocker, demands a truthful account of the events at the Abbey Grange, and recognizes that Crocker is responsible for the killing. He concludes that Crocker's actions may have been legitimate self-defense, tests his willingness to protect Mary, and conducts an informal trial that results in Crocker's acquittal.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE SECOND STAIN

Sherlock Holmes receives Lord Bellinger and Trelawney Hope at Baker Street and agrees to investigate the disappearance of the letter after they disclose its political significance. He reasons that the letter was taken between 7:30 and 11:30 in the evening and begins looking for three leading international agents: Oberstein, La Rothiere, and Eduardo Lucas.

My friend has so often astonished me in the course of our

Sherlock Holmes reads an account of Eduardo Lucas's murder and concludes that it must be connected with the Whitehall Terrace political incident. He receives Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, refuses to reveal confidential details about the stolen paper, and later suspects that she was concealing her true motive. He then goes to Godolphin Street to investigate.

All that day and the next and the next Holmes was in a mood which

Sherlock Holmes studies the murder investigation while remaining chiefly concerned with tracing the missing letter and preventing a European catastrophe. At the room where Lucas was killed, he recognizes that the drugget was turned and discovers a concealed floor cavity, but finds it empty. He leaves with an undisclosed object and goes with Dr. John Watson toward Whitehall Terrace.

When we arrived at the residence of the European Secretary it was

Sherlock Holmes confronts Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, reveals that he knows about her dealings with Eduardo Lucas and the theft of the political document, and persuades her to surrender it. He hides the document in Trelawney Hope’s despatch-box and later tells Trelawney Hope and the Prime Minister that he knew it was nowhere else.
