Sherlock Holmes in His Last Bow

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1908-04-17 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is an alive, generally well private and consulting detective, investigator, and friend and professional associate of Dr. John Watson. Sought for difficult criminal and national-security matters, he works through close observation, physical traces, documents, codes, advertisements, experiments, disguises, and tightly reasoned hypotheses. He dislikes publicity, can be impatient with less alert minds, and lives and investigates with irregular habits, scientific experiments, music, and a revolver; Watson assists him and is his close companion. Mycroft Holmes is his brother. Across the records, Holmes collaborates at times with inspectors while also pursuing independent lines of inquiry. In the Wisteria Lodge affair, he interprets messages, footprints, household details, and ritual evidence to expose Garcia’s enterprise, Don Murillo, and the danger to Miss Burnet. In the Bruce-Partington plans investigation, he traces Cadogan West’s death and the stolen plans through railway evidence, a house over the Underground, coded advertisements, and confessions, leading to Oberstein’s arrest. While his health is weakened, he rests at Poldhu Cottage with Watson but solves the Devil’s Foot tragedy by rejecting supernatural explanations, studying footprints and chemical residue, and deciding not to report Sterndale after hearing his account. He protects endangered people in further cases: he deciphers Italian signals and summons Emilia Lucca in the Red Circle matter; tracks Lady Frances Carfax through records and suspects, then rescues her from a coffin before burial; and feigns a fatal contagious illness to draw Culverton Smith into confessing, with Watson and Inspector Morton securing the arrest. His methods also include a small, efficient private organisation and the use of newspaper agony columns and a scrapbook. Later, having intended permanent retirement on a small South Downs farm, Holmes divides his leisure between philosophy, agriculture, and bee culture, writing Practical Handbook of Bee Culture, with Some Observations upon the Segregation of the Queen. Yet he places his intellectual and practical activity at the Government’s disposal when war demands it. Under the alias Altamont, he infiltrates Von Bork’s German espionage network for two years, supplies deliberately unreliable information, captures Von Bork, and exposes the operation with Watson beside him. Despite occasional rheumatism, the record closes with Holmes serving English people as a patriotic agent after a life of investigation and planned retirement.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

21 sections; each heading opens the text

opening

Sherlock Holmes is described as alive and well, though occasionally crippled by attacks of rheumatism. He has lived for many years on a small farm on the Downs near Eastbourne, dividing his time between philosophy and agriculture, and had intended his retirement to be permanent until the German war led him to serve the Government.

The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge / 1. The Singular Experience of Mr. John Scott Eccles

Sherlock Holmes receives and replies to the telegram from John Scott Eccles, then questions Eccles about his experience. He examines the note found by Inspector Baynes, adds observations about its seal and scissors, and agrees to collaborate with the investigation.

We sat for some time in silence after our visitors had left. Holmes

Sherlock Holmes examines the events surrounding Garcia, Scott Eccles, and Wisteria Lodge. He theorizes that Eccles was selected as a respectable witness who could establish an alibi for Garcia, interprets the mysterious message as a signal and assignation, and uses a list of nearby large houses to narrow the investigation.

2. The Tiger of San Pedro

Sherlock Holmes examines the grounds and the kitchen at Wisteria Lodge, identifying a number twelve shoe print and judging the burned bones to be those of a lamb or kid. He becomes interested in the case but follows his own investigation while Inspector Baynes follows another line. After reading of the arrest of Garcia's alleged cook, Holmes warns Baynes that he may be on the wrong track.

“Just sit down in that chair, Watson,” said Sherlock Holmes when we had

Sherlock Holmes explains his deductions about Garcia's criminal enterprise, Garcia's household, High Gable, and Miss Burnet's disappearance to Dr. Watson. He plans to enter High Gable at night through the roof of an outhouse with Watson to investigate the mystery.

But it was not destined that our investigation should have so

Sherlock Holmes arranges for the discharged gardener to watch the gate and recover Miss Burnet when she breaks away at the station. He learns from her statement that Henderson is Don Murillo and works with Inspector Baynes to connect the coded note, Garcia's murder, and the attempted murder of Miss Burnet. Later, he explains the mulatto cook's return and identifies the kitchen's sacrifices as voodoo ritual practices.

The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans

Sherlock Holmes learns from Mycroft that Arthur Cadogan West was found dead with seven of the ten stolen Bruce-Partington plans in his possession. He considers possible explanations for West’s actions and death, agrees to investigate the case, and sets out with Dr. Watson and Lestrade for Aldgate Station.

An hour later Holmes, Lestrade and I stood upon the Underground

Sherlock Holmes examines the scene near Aldgate Station and infers that Cadogan West's body was probably carried on the roof of a train and fell off where the line curved over the points. He visits Woolwich, questions witnesses, inspects the government office, and develops the hypothesis that West may have pursued the thief of the Bruce-Partington plans. He asks Mycroft Holmes for a list of foreign spies and international agents in England.

Surely enough, a note awaited us at Baker Street. A government

Sherlock Holmes deduces that Cadogan West’s body was placed on the roof of a train through a window overlooking the Underground railway at Caulfield Gardens. He burglarizes Hugo Oberstein’s house, discovers advertisement-column messages, and uses a false message to lure Oberstein. Holmes captures Colonel Valentine Walter, obtains his confession, and sends a letter designed to bring Oberstein to London, where he is arrested.

The Adventure of the Devil’s Foot

Sherlock Holmes is ordered by Dr. Moore Agar to stop working and rest because his health is failing from constant hard work. He stays with Dr. John Watson in a cottage near Poldhu Bay, but investigates the Tredannick Wartha tragedy after Mr. Roundhay and Mortimer Tregennis appeal to him. He questions Mortimer, visits the house, examines the room and garden, and concludes that no new factor has yet appeared to explain the events.

It was not until long after we were back in Poldhu Cottage that Holmes

Sherlock Holmes stops brooding at Poldhu Cottage and walks along the cliffs with Dr. John Watson while defining what is known about the case. He rules out diabolical intrusions, concludes that human agency was involved, examines Mortimer Tregennis's movements through his footprints, and postpones the case until more evidence appears.

I may have commented upon my friend’s power of mental detachment, but

Sherlock Holmes questions Dr. Leon Sterndale about his return from Plymouth and investigates Mortimer Tregennis’s death. He examines the bedroom window and lamp, identifies ashes and brownish powder on the lamp’s talc shield, and concludes that a substance burned in the room produced a poisonous atmosphere. He tests the substance with Dr. John Watson and reasons that Mortimer Tregennis was probably responsible for the first tragedy.

Fortunately, there is one man in England who knows all about it, and I

Sherlock Holmes summons Dr. Leon Sterndale and confronts him with the charge of killing Mortimer Tregennis. He reveals that the gravel on the windowsill, Sterndale's movements, the lamp, and the powder residue led to his conclusion. After hearing Sterndale's explanation, Holmes decides not to interfere or report him.

The Adventure of the Red Circle / PART I

Sherlock Holmes investigates Mrs. Warren’s unusual lodger after hearing that the man stays hidden, prints brief messages, and has apparently been replaced by a woman. He deduces that the lodgers are communicating through the Daily Gazette and recognizes the flashing signals as Italian warnings of danger.

PART II

Sherlock Holmes follows the signal message from the Howe Street flat, joins Gregson and Mr. Leverton, and helps investigate the premises. He identifies the dead man as Giuseppe Gorgiano’s likely killer’s victim, uses the window candle to summon Emilia Lucca, and elicits her account of the events.

The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax

Sherlock Holmes investigates Lady Frances Carfax's disappearance through her bank records and correspondence, then sends Dr. Watson to Lausanne and other locations while he remains in London. He identifies Dr. Shlessinger as Holy Peters after confirming a distinctive injury to his left ear and concludes that Lady Frances is probably in danger.

But neither the official police nor Holmes’s own small but very

Sherlock Holmes directs the investigation into Lady Frances Carfax’s disappearance and sends Philip Green to watch for further jewellery sales. He confronts Henry Peters at No. 36, Poultney Square, initially misinterprets the coffin’s purpose, then recognizes that it was specially made to conceal Lady Frances and rescues her before burial.

The Adventure of the Dying Detective

Sherlock Holmes is found gravely ill, wasted, feverish, and apparently delirious, but he remains imperious and determined to control the situation. He prevents Dr. Watson from leaving until six o'clock, insists on keeping his distance because he claims the illness is contagious, and directs Watson to fetch Culverton Smith. Holmes also reacts violently when Watson touches a small black-and-white ivory box.

Lower Burke Street proved to be a line of fine houses lying in the

Sherlock Holmes pretends to be desperately ill in order to lure Culverton Smith into confessing. He hides Dr. Watson behind his bed, reveals that he has been acting, and helps Inspector Morton secure Smith's arrest.

His Last Bow: The War Service of Sherlock Holmes

Altamont is presented as an Irish-American agent who sells German espionage information and demands £500 for delivering a copy of the British naval signals code. The man who arrives under his name is actually Sherlock Holmes in disguise, carrying a copy of Practical Handbook of Bee Culture instead of the promised code.

“Another glass, Watson!” said Mr. Sherlock Holmes as he extended the

Sherlock Holmes captures Von Bork after posing for two years as the American operative Altamont. He removes dossiers from Von Bork’s safe, explains that much of the information supplied to the German government was deliberately unreliable, and takes Von Bork toward Scotland Yard with John Watson.

Sherlock Holmes in The Valley of Fear

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1914-09 to 1915-05 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is a celebrated, independent amateur detective and crime consultant whose exceptionally active intellect and remarkable powers drive him to investigate difficult cases while helping the police. He is Dr. Watson’s friend and companion, works with Inspector MacDonald and White Mason at Birlstone, and remains loyal to officials when they share a case. He also opposes Professor Moriarty, has visited Moriarty’s rooms three times and once ransacked his papers, yet keeps faith with informant Fred Porlock by refusing to trace him. The account begins when Holmes deciphers Porlock’s cipher using an older edition of Whitaker’s Almanac. The message warns that Douglas is in danger at Birlstone. When John Douglas is reported murdered, Holmes links the warning to possible activity by Moriarty’s organization and travels to investigate. At Birlstone he scrutinizes the study, body, weapon, window, moat, marks, card, footprints, clothing, and especially a missing dumb-bell. He challenges the theory of an outside killer, exposes inconsistencies in Cecil Barker’s account of the candle and lamp, and shows that Barker’s slipper could have made the blood mark on the sill. Holmes concludes that Barker and Mrs. Douglas are concealing facts, though he does not initially decide that they committed murder. By reasoning that the murder occurred earlier than claimed and that the missing dumb-bell was central, Holmes conducts a solitary test: he places a sodden bundle in the moat and uses a proposed draining to provoke its recovery. He identifies Barker as the retriever, finds the dumb-bell, and reveals that Douglas is alive and hidden in the manor; the body could not be Douglas because Douglas’s clothes were recovered from the moat. Holmes urges Douglas to remain alert, warning of danger from American enemies and from English law. In the end, after an enigmatic note and news of Douglas’s death, Holmes judges that Moriarty organized Douglas’s murder from London and says Moriarty can be defeated if given time to plan.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

10 sections; each heading opens the text

PART I / Chapter I

Sherlock Holmes examines a cipher message from Fred Porlock and reasons that it refers to numbered words in a large, standardized book printed in double columns. He correctly identifies an older edition of Whitaker’s Almanac as the key and decodes a warning about danger threatening Douglas at Birlstone.

Chapter II

Sherlock Holmes is interested rather than surprised when he learns that John Douglas has been murdered, because Porlock’s anonymous warning had predicted danger to a certain person. He explains his suspicions about Professor Moriarty’s criminal organization, wealth, and possible connection to the murder, then travels with Inspector MacDonald to Birlstone to investigate.

Chapter IV

Holmes travels with Dr. Watson to Birlstone and listens closely to White Mason’s account of the case. He examines the shotgun, moat, window, body, blood mark, card, ink, footprints, and dumb-bell, and suggests that the branded mark and card may point to a secret society. He finds White Mason’s outside-killer theory interesting but unconvincing and continues seeking further facts.

Chapter V

Sherlock Holmes questions Cecil Barker about the candle and lamp in the study. He points out that Barker said the candle was lit when he entered, but that the candle was later out and the lamp was burning.

Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait

Sherlock Holmes questions Mrs. Douglas about the words associated with Mr. Douglas's past and examines Cecil Barker's carpet slippers. He places one slipper on the blood mark on the study window sill and finds that it exactly corresponds, showing that Barker could have made the mark himself.

Chapter VI

Sherlock Holmes says he wants no confidential information from Mrs. Douglas or Barker because it could become awkward if they were arrested for conspiracy and murder. He identifies the missing dumb-bell as highly important and argues that Barker’s account is a lie corroborated by Mrs. Douglas. Holmes suspects they are conspiring to conceal the truth, but he remains uncertain whether they committed the murder and plans to spend an evening alone in the study.

It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back

Sherlock Holmes listens to MacDonald's theory but argues that the murder occurred half an hour earlier than reported and that Mrs. Douglas and Barker helped conceal the truth. He undertakes a solitary investigation centered on why Mr. Douglas developed his athletic frame with a single dumb-bell, then returns appearing to question his own sanity.

Chapter VII

Sherlock Holmes advises Inspector MacDonald and White Mason to abandon their search for the mysterious cyclist while he verifies his own theory. He finds the missing dumb-bell and uses it to test the moat, then announces that the moat-draining plan has caused the person who hid the bundle to retrieve it. Holmes identifies Cecil Barker as the retriever and concludes that John Douglas is alive and should tell the complete story.

“That’s the past, Mr. Douglas,” said Sherlock Holmes quietly. “What we

Holmes explains that the body found at Birlstone Manor could not be John Douglas because Douglas's suit of clothes had been found in the moat. He inferred that Douglas was concealed somewhere in the manor and warns that Douglas may face dangers from his American enemies as well as English law.

Epilogue

Sherlock Holmes warned that John Douglas faced greater danger in England than the danger he had escaped. After receiving an enigmatic note and hearing of Douglas's death, Holmes concluded that the death was murder organized from London by Moriarty. He said Moriarty could be defeated but asked for time to plan a response.

Sherlock Holmes in The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle · 1921-10 · the work’s page · read it where Sherlock Holmes first appears

Abstract written by a model

Sherlock Holmes is an imaginary, famous consulting and private detective, a professional investigator whose adventures debut in A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four. Based at Baker Street for much of his active practice, he works closely with Dr. John Watson, his friend, companion, confidential partner, and frequent assistant. Holmes is defined by logical analysis, intellectual deduction, acute senses, an unusually retentive memory for trifles, trained observation, and a habit of using his head rather than his heart. He maintains confidential records, seeks no public credit, represents justice through his work, and uses associates such as Shinwell Johnson, Langdale Pike, Mercer, and the police when useful. His characteristic possessions and methods include pipes, a tobacco-slipper, a notebook and index volume, disguises, practical jokes, forensic microscopy, staged deceptions, and direct personal risk. The records show him facing threats, exhaustion, and injury while continuing to investigate. In the Baron Gruner matter, he tries to save Violet de Merville, is attacked and wounded, and obtains Gruner's incriminating book through a calculated burglary. He then resolves varied cases: exposing Godfrey Emsworth's condition, recovering the Mazarin Stone from Count Sylvius, protecting Mrs. Maberley from a manuscript theft, explaining the Ferguson household's supposed vampirism, uncovering James Winter's fraud against Nathan Garrideb, and proving that Mrs. Gibson framed Miss Dunbar before taking her own life. Later cases emphasize his willingness to challenge hidden wrongdoing and seemingly strange events. He traces Professor Presbury's transformation to Langur serum, identifies Cyanea capillata as the cause of deaths at the Sussex coast, responds sympathetically to the veiled lodger's confession, exposes concealment at Shoscombe Old Place, and discovers that Josiah Amberley used a sealed strong-room and gas to kill. After twenty-three years of active practice, including seventeen years of cooperation with Watson, Holmes retires to his little Sussex home, keeps bees, yet continues to investigate when summoned. A preface presents him as a popular fictional detective who was ended, revived, and finally bid farewell amid continuing public interest.

Narrative, section by section written by a model

33 sections; each heading opens the text

PREFACE

Sherlock Holmes is presented as a popular fictional detective whose adventures began in A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four. Arthur Conan Doyle says that Holmes was once brought to an end but was later revived, and he now bids Holmes farewell while acknowledging the public's continuing interest in him.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS CLIENT

Sherlock Holmes agrees to investigate Baron Gruner after hearing that Gruner intends to marry Violet de Merville. He visits Gruner, warns him to abandon the marriage, and receives veiled threats involving Le Brun. Holmes also calls on Shinwell Johnson to gather information about Gruner.

We found him sure enough, a huge, coarse, red-faced, scorbutic man,

Sherlock Holmes questions Kitty Winter about Adelbert Gruner and learns that she may be able to help stop Gruner's marriage. He considers arranging for Kitty to meet Gruner's intended bride and is told where Gruner may keep his brown leather book.

I did not see Holmes again until the following evening, when we dined

Sherlock Holmes visits Violet de Merville with Miss Winter and pleads with Violet to reconsider her engagement to Baron Gruner. When Violet rejects his warnings, he restrains Miss Winter from attacking her, then decides that a fresh approach is necessary.

And it did. Their blow fell--or his blow rather, for never could I

Sherlock Holmes is attacked by two men and suffers two lacerated scalp wounds and considerable bruising, though he deliberately exaggerates the seriousness of his condition. He sends Dr. John Watson to investigate Baron Adelbert Gruner and secretly joins the operation, appearing at Gruner's house in bloody bandages before escaping through a window.

Holmes was seated in his familiar chair, looking very pale and

Sherlock Holmes, pale and exhausted after the evening's events, explains that he used Dr. Watson's distraction and the blue saucer to steal Baron Adelbert Gruner's incriminating book. He says the book is necessary to break Violet de Merville's attachment to Gruner and is later threatened with prosecution for burglary, though he has not stood trial.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLANCHED SOLDIER

Sherlock Holmes receives James M. Dodd at his rooms and identifies Dodd's South African service and Imperial Yeomanry background through observation. He listens to Dodd's account of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance and begins investigating the matter through Dodd's testimony.

My client had paused as one in deep emotion.

Sherlock Holmes listens to the client's account and questions him about the newspaper being read by the little bearded man, treating that detail as essential.

Such was the problem which my visitor laid before me. It presented, as

Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. James M. Dodd about the servants, food deliveries, local inquiries, Godfrey Emsworth's appearance, and the circumstances of his confinement. He infers that Godfrey may have leprosy, identifies the odour of disinfectant on Ralph's gloves, and writes "Leprosy" on a scrap of paper to force Colonel Emsworth to disclose the secret. Holmes brings Sir James Saunders to provide a medical opinion and explains how he eliminated criminality and insanity before adopting the leprosy theory.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE MAZARIN STONE

Sherlock Holmes investigates the missing Mazarin Stone and tracks Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton. He uses disguises, a wax dummy, and psychological pressure to confront Sylvius, learn the stone's location, and arrange for the criminals to choose between surrendering the stone and being arrested.

Holmes withdrew, picking up his violin from the corner as he passed. A

Holmes disguises himself as the dummy and listens from behind a curtain while Count Sylvius and Sam Merton discuss the stone. He suddenly seizes the Mazarin stone, threatens the criminals with a revolver, summons the police, and explains how he outwitted them. Later, he places the stone in Lord Cantlemere's pocket as a practical joke before recovering it.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GABLES

Holmes is threatened by Steve Dixie because he is investigating the Harrow Weald case. He identifies connections among Steve, Barney Stockdale, Susan, and an unknown wealthy woman, questions Mrs. Maberley and Susan, protects the house, and suspects that Douglas Maberley's recently arrived luggage contains the object sought by the conspirators.

When I met my friend in his room early next morning, I was conscious

Sherlock Holmes goes with Dr. Watson to The Three Gables after receiving the telegram. He identifies the burglary as an attempt to recover Douglas Maberley's manuscript, confronts Isadora Klein, obtains her admission that she ordered the crime, and arranges for her to give £5,000 to Mrs. Maberley.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE SUSSEX VAMPIRE

Holmes initially dismisses supernatural vampirism as lunacy but considers the possibility that the case involves a living person with vampiric habits. After questioning Robert Ferguson about the family, the wife, the baby, and Jack, he forms provisional theories and agrees to travel to Lamberley with Watson to investigate.

It was evening of a dull, foggy November day when, having left our bags

Sherlock Holmes visits the Ferguson farmhouse with Dr. John Watson and investigates the apparent vampirism. He deduces that Ferguson's wife saved the baby by sucking poison from the child's wound and that Jacky Ferguson was responsible for the attempted poisoning. He concludes that Jacky should spend a year at sea and later writes that the matter has been satisfactorily concluded.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE THREE GARRIDEBS

Sherlock Holmes is approached by John Garrideb and Nathan Garrideb regarding the search for another Garrideb. He detects that John has lied about his background and the search, noting his worn English clothing, lack of newspaper advertisements, and false reference to Dr. Lysander Starr. Holmes visits Nathan, questions him about the inheritance and his collection, and agrees that Nathan should travel to Birmingham to meet Howard Garrideb.

I noticed that my friend's face cleared when the American left the

Sherlock Holmes investigates the American's identity and learns from Scotland Yard that John Garrideb is James Winter, alias Killer Evans. He traces the connection between Rodger Prescott, the former tenant of Nathan Garrideb's apartment, and a hidden counterfeiting operation. Holmes and Dr. John Watson ambush Evans, disarm and subdue him, and arrange for the Yard to take him away.

THE PROBLEM OF THOR BRIDGE

Sherlock Holmes agrees to examine the case against Miss Dunbar after receiving a letter from Neil Gibson. He questions Gibson about his relationship with Miss Dunbar, accuses him of giving false information, and bluffs him into revealing the history of his marriage to Maria Pinto.

"Then came Miss Grace Dunbar. She answered our advertisement and

Holmes tells the millionaire that he does not blame him for feeling regard for Grace but would blame him for expressing it because she was under his protection. He criticizes the millionaire's conduct and says he is concerned with the case only for the young lady's sake.

To my surprise the Gold King took the reproof with equanimity.

Mr. Holmes considers an accidental shooting during a struggle a possible alternative to deliberate murder. He plans to obtain the necessary permits and travel to Winchester to see Miss Dunbar.

There was some delay in the official pass, and instead of reaching

Sherlock Holmes visits Thor Place with Dr. Watson and Sergeant Coventry to examine Mrs. Gibson's killing. He questions the evidence, notices a chipped place on the lower edge of Thor Bridge's parapet, and argues that the pistol found in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe may have been planted to incriminate her.

We were compelled to spend the night at Winchester, as the formalities

Sherlock Holmes interviews Miss Dunbar at Winchester and accepts her account of her innocent relationship with Neil Gibson. He recognizes that the fresh chip in the bridge stonework is a crucial clue, reproduces the weapon's disposal method, and concludes that Mrs. Gibson framed Miss Dunbar before taking her own life.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN

Sherlock Holmes is consulted by Trevor Bennett and Edith Presbury about Professor Presbury's strange behavior. He considers Roy's attacks, the secret letters, the wooden box, and the dates of the incidents to be connected, and plans to visit Presbury in Camford with Dr. Watson.

Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an

Holmes visits Professor Presbury in Camford with Watson, claiming that he was summoned, in order to establish personal contact. After Presbury reacts violently, Holmes learns from Mr. Bennett about Dorak and Miss Presbury's danger, investigates Dorak through Mercer, and develops a theory that Presbury takes a strong drug at nine-day intervals.

In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.

Sherlock Holmes identifies the significance of Professor Presbury's nine-day symptoms, his changed knuckles, the dog, and the ivy. He witnesses Presbury's animal-like behavior, investigates the locked box, reads H. Lowenstein's letter, and concludes that Langur serum caused the transformation. He plans to write to Lowenstein and hold him criminally responsible for distributing the poisons.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE

Mr. Holmes, living in retirement near the Sussex coast, discovers Fitzroy McPherson dying and takes charge of the initial investigation. He examines the beach, the footprints, McPherson’s belongings, and the correspondence connecting McPherson with Maud Bellamy.

A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had

Sherlock Holmes investigates the unexplained death of Fitzroy McPherson and initially considers Ian Murdoch a possible suspect. After learning of the dog's death and recalling information from J. G. Wood's Out of Doors, he identifies Cyanea capillata in the bathing-pool and explains the deaths and attacks as jellyfish stings.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER

Sherlock Holmes is summoned by Mrs. Merrilow to hear the confession of her veiled lodger. He recalls investigating the Abbas Parva tragedy indirectly and having suspected that the coroner's verdict of death from misadventure did not explain all the evidence.

We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her

Sherlock Holmes expresses sympathy for the unnamed woman and asks about Leonardo and the five-clawed club. He tells her that her life is not her own and urges her to endure her suffering. Two days later, he shows John Watson a blue bottle of prussic acid sent to him by post.

THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE

Sherlock Holmes examines microscopic evidence in another case before hearing John Mason's concerns about Shoscombe Old Place. He theorizes that Sir Robert may have killed Lady Beatrice, concealed her body, and arranged for someone to impersonate her, then travels with Dr. Watson to investigate while posing as a fisherman.

In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our

Sherlock Holmes investigates the apparent illness and identity of Lady Beatrice at Shoscombe Old Place. He uses the black spaniel to show that the woman in the carriage is a stranger, finds Lady Beatrice's body in an ancestral coffin, and compels Sir Robert to explain the concealment and personation.

THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN

Sherlock Holmes receives Josiah Amberley's case through the Yard but initially considers it commonplace. He sends Dr. John Watson to The Haven because he is occupied with the case of the two Coptic Patriarchs, then analyzes Watson's report and points out important details Watson missed.

In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty

Sherlock Holmes arranged for Josiah Amberley to follow the forged telegram to Little Purlington so that he could examine Amberley's house without interruption. He discovered the gas pipe leading into the sealed strong-room, identified the wall message, confronted Amberley about the bodies, and turned his findings over to Inspector MacKinnon and the police.
